title: A third hospital at SR 60 and 66th Avenue? Where the plan stands and how neighbors get a say.
seoTitle: Vero Beach Third Hospital at SR 60 & 66th Ave: Status
description: A five-story hospital is proposed near SR 60 and 66th Avenue west of Vero Beach. What is planned, what the county must change, and how homeowners can weigh in.
dek: No application has been filed and no vote has been taken. But county commissioners are already debating the height rule that would make it possible, and that matters to everyone who lives nearby.
keywords: Indian River County hospital height exemption

body.text: Indian River County has two hospitals today: Cleveland Clinic Indian River Hospital in Vero Beach and Orlando Health Sebastian River Hospital in Sebastian. A group of investors wants to add a third, west of both, near State Road 60 and 66th Avenue.

The idea has been in front of the County Commission twice this fall, most recently in early October. If you live in west Vero, near the 66th Avenue corridor or anywhere on SR 60, here is what is known, what is not, and when the public gets to speak.

body.title: Where it stands today
body.text: No formal application has been filed, and commissioners have not voted. The project's backers are gauging the board's interest first. If they do apply, WQCS reports the project would need at least seven public hearings before construction could begin.

Former county commissioner Tim Zorc and former county attorney Dylan Reingold have spoken for the project. The hospital operator has not been named. Zorc has said the landowner holds 75 acres near SR 60 and 66th Avenue, close to Indian River State College's Mueller Campus.

The early plans describe a building of about 250,000 to 260,000 square feet, five stories tall. Zorc has put the possible investment in the $300 million range. No bed count, construction date or emergency room layout has been confirmed in public.

That size is the sticking point. WQCS reported that current rules in that area cap buildings at 35 feet tall and 60,000 square feet. The proposal would need a height exemption for five stories in an area now limited to three, along with changes to the county's comprehensive plan and land development rules.

In September, WQCS reported that commissioners agreed the county needs a third hospital but were not ready to move ahead without more talk about height. Commissioner Joseph Flescher said the hospital should be smaller, pointing to successful hospitals of three and four stories. Zorc answered that a shorter building would need about five more variances and could be hard to fit on the site.

At the October discussion, Commissioner Laura Moss questioned whether the county has shown the need for a third hospital, and said the county should not create an incentive before that need is established. Commissioner Joseph Earman said the county's job is to check zoning and code compliance, not to decide whether the community needs another hospital.

Supporters made their case on access. Zorc cited an April 2025 report that put the area about 108 beds short compared with Brevard and St. Lucie counties. Advocate Dan Sorrow said a western hospital could shorten ambulance trips for people in the west county, and that freight trains at crossings west of US 1 can add 7 to 10 minutes of waiting.
Why the height rule matters beyond one building

This is the part homeowners near the site should watch. The county attorney has raised concerns that changing the height rules could open the door to other five-story projects nearby, because of Florida's Live Local Act.

The county attorney's office has worked with Reingold on wording meant to keep the exemption limited to a hospital. Moss said she was not yet convinced that wording solves the problem. In short, the details of how the rule is written may matter as much as the hospital itself.

Approval from the county would not be the last step. IRC Media reported that Florida no longer requires a traditional Certificate of Need for a general hospital, but the project would still need licensing, design and construction approval from the Agency for Health Care Administration.
What to do if you live nearby

items: Know where you are. Pull up a map and see how close your street is to SR 60 and 66th Avenue. The closer you are, the more the height and traffic questions affect you.
Watch the County Commission agendas. They are posted ahead of each meeting at indianriver.gov. Look for items on hospital height, the comprehensive plan or land development regulations.

Learn the difference between a discussion and a hearing. What has happened so far is discussion. Public hearings come later, if an application is filed, and that is when your comments go into the record.

Speak or write in. You can make public comment at a commission meeting or email the commissioners. Short, specific comments about traffic, drainage, building height or emergency access on your street carry the most weight.
Keep an eye on traffic plans. A large hospital brings ambulances, staff shifts and visitors. If the project moves forward, ask how SR 60 and 66th Avenue access would be handled.

body.text: Whether you want a hospital closer to home, worry about five stories down the road, or both, now is the quiet stage. It is the best time to learn the facts before the hearings start.

faq.q: Is a third hospital being built in Indian River County?
faq.a: Not yet. Investors have proposed a hospital near SR 60 and 66th Avenue, but as of early October 2026 no formal application had been filed and commissioners had not voted.

faq.q: Where would the new Vero Beach hospital be?
faq.a: Near State Road 60 and 66th Avenue, west of Vero Beach, close to Indian River State College's Mueller Campus. The landowner holds about 75 acres there.

faq.q: How tall would the proposed hospital be?
faq.a: Early plans call for about five stories. Current rules in that area limit buildings to 35 feet and three stories, so the county would need to grant a height exemption.

faq.q: Who is behind the proposed hospital on SR 60?
faq.a: Former county commissioner Tim Zorc and former county attorney Dylan Reingold have spoken for the project. The hospital operator has not been publicly named.

faq.q: When can the public comment on the new hospital?
faq.a: Public comment is allowed at County Commission meetings now. If an application is filed, WQCS reports the project would go through at least seven public hearings before construction.
